title: Bamidbar: counted by name (Numbers 1:2)
hookLine: a census "by their polls", each person counted, not just a total

cards: Six hundred three thousand, five hundred fifty. That's the total the book of Numbers gives for its first census: men twenty and older, ready to go out with the army. It's the kind of number that makes eyes glaze.
A stadium, a city, a statistic. And yet the Torah's instructions for getting there are oddly personal. Not count the tents.

Not estimate the crowd. Something slower, one person at a time. Before the wilderness journey even begins, God asks Moses to stop and count, and the way the count is described says more than the total.

teach.h: ACCORDING TO THE NUMBER OF NAMES.
teach.b: Numbers, chapter one, verse two. Take the sum of the whole congregation, by families, by fathers' houses, "according to the number of names, every male, by their polls." Polls is old English for heads.

teach.h: BY THEIR POLLS: HEAD BY HEAD.
teach.b: The Hebrew is l'gulgelotam, by their skulls, head by head. And the number of names: each one counted as a someone, not a something.
Rashi, at the very first verse, asks why this people gets counted so often: once leaving Egypt, once after the golden calf, and now again.
His answer: because they're dear to God, God counts them often, the way someone counts a treasure, not to learn the total, but to touch each piece again.
Other commentators, like Nachmanides, read the counting by name as a way of giving each person dignity: you didn't just pass through a gate, you stood before Moses and Aaron and said who you were.

There's a flip side, and Jewish custom takes it seriously. The Talmud warns against counting Jews by number directly, and there's a story of King Saul counting his soldiers by pebbles or lambs instead.

So when a congregation checks whether ten adults are present for a prayer quorum, the custom is not to say one, two, three. Some say a verse of ten Hebrew words, one word per person. Others count not one, not two.
Both come from the same instinct.
A person is never only a number.
Count every head, and never reduce a head to a count.

how: Jewish custom avoids counting people by number; to check for a minyan of ten, some recite a ten-word verse, one word per person, or count "not one, not two." The census of Numbers 1 is read each year in the portion Bamidbar.

practice: Think through your week: the person at the front desk, the bus driver on your route, the neighbor two doors down, the new person at work you've been calling hey, you.
Pick one whose name you don't know, or have forgotten and feel shy to ask, and picture their face. Decide how you'd ask; something simple works: I'm sorry, I've never asked your name.
